english_translation: My sibling is reading, so we are speaking in whispers.

dialogue.shona: Hanzvadzi yangu iri kuverenga saka tiri kutaura tichizevezera.
dialogue.english: My sibling is reading, so we are speaking in whispers.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Hanzvadzi [hanzvadzi] • yangu [yangu] • iri [iri] • kuverenga [to / at verenga] • saka [so / therefore] • tiri [tiri] • kutaura [to / at taura] • tichizevezera [tichizevezera]

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('yangu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'yangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

grammar_notes.title: Pointing Out Things: Demonstratives ('iri' = 'this / that / here')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, words for 'this/these' and 'that/those' (like 'iri') come AFTER the noun they point to and mirror the noun's group! Near demonstratives ('this / these / right here') repeat the noun class vowel: 'mwana uyu' (this child), 'nyama iyi' (this meat), 'kapu iyi' (this cup), 'bhuku iri' (this book), 'zvinhu izvi' (these things). Replacing the final vowel with '-o' shifts the meaning to 'that / those / there': 'uyo' (that person), 'iyo' (that one), 'uko' (over there).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Near Demonstrative ('uyu/iyi/iri/ichi/izvi' = this/these) | replace final vowel with '-o' ('uyo/iyo/iro/icho/izvo' = that/those)

cultural_notes.title: Respecting Study Time at Home & Speaking in Whispers ('Kuzevezera')
cultural_notes.content: Notice the word 'hanzvadzi'—which means a brother to a sister, or a sister to a brother! When a sibling is studying or reading for exams ('iri kuverenga'), family members lower their voices to a whisper ('tichizevezera') to support their concentration.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new family sentence into English: 'Hanzvadzi yangu inoshanda muguta reHarare.'
options: My parents live at the rural homestead in Masvingo.
My friend passed all her school examinations this year.
The baby is sleeping quietly inside the bedroom.
My sibling works in the city of Harare.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My sibling works in the city of Harare.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Hanzvadzi yangu' = 'My sibling (brother/sister)', 'inoshanda' = 'works', 'muguta reHarare' = 'in the city of Harare'.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this sentence using the Present Progressive ('is reading right now'): 'Shamwari yangu ______ bhuku idzva.'
active_exercises.explanation: 'Shamwari' uses the progressive form 'iri ku-' + '-verenga' (read) to mean 'is reading right now'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new greeting into English: 'Masikati amai, maswera zvakanaka here?'
options: Good morning Grandmother, did you sleep well?
Good afternoon Mother, did you spend the day well?
Good evening everyone inside the house.
Thank you very much for helping us today.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Good afternoon Mother, did you spend the day well?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Masikati amai' = 'Good afternoon Mother', 'maswera zvakanaka here?' = 'have you spent the day well?'.
